LESSON GOALS
•	 To understand simple stories and conversations.
•	 To ask and answer questions about familiar topics 
(personal information, clothes, colours, weather, etc.).
•	 To talk about things you can see in different places 
in the world and things you can buy or do in a shop.
•	 To understand obligation, lack of obligation and advice.

3.– WORKSHEET: WHAT SHOULD YOU WEAR? (P.10) (8’)
What Should You Wear?
10
MATERIALS
•	 Crayons or pencils
NOTE: if you collected your Ss’ books during the booklet 
activity, have them ask you for it now by saying “Can I have 
my book please?”; otherwise, ask them to take it out of their 
bag. Explain the activity before giving out the books/asking Ss 
to take them out since they might get distracted.
This worksheet consists of two activities. First, Ss must match 
the weather conditions on the first row with the clothing items 
on the second row. Then they have to draw suitable items to 
wear when it’s hot in the blank box.
Review the different concepts pointing at the worksheet. You 
should start by asking, “What’s the weather like?” and have 
the Ss respond, “It’s windy!”, etc. Review the items by asking, 
“What is this?/ What are these?”, and eliciting the names of 
the items (gloves, sunglasses, umbrella, jacket).
Then, point to a weather condition and ask a S, for example, 
“What should you wear if it’s snowy?” to which the S should 
reply, “If it’s snowy, you should wear a pair of gloves.” Continue 
in the same manner until you have finished the first part of the 
exercise. Allow Ss to talk about any other kind of clothing that 
can be worn if it is correct.
Once you have completed the first part, point to the image 
depicting hot weather and ask, “What’s the weather like?”. Ss 
should answer, “It’s hot.”. Ask, “What should you wear if it’s 
hot?”. Let Ss give as many answers as possible and encourage 
them to draw one or two items in the blank box.

NOTE: adapt the target language when asking about rainy: 
“What should you take when it’s rainy?”, “When it’s rainy, 
you should take an umbrella.”

5.– ACTIVITY 5: RIGHT OR WRONG? (6’)
> How to Play
Show the Ss different pages from the Big Book and say a 
sentence about them. The Ss then have to decide if it is right 
or wrong.
> Warm-Up
Start off with some easy statements. Say for example, “Paul 
is a girl. Is that right or wrong?”. The Ss should then reply, “No, 
that’s wrong! Paul is a boy.” Say two or three more statements 
and make them correct you.
NOTE: if your Ss are familiar with the target language, you 
may skip this step.
> Main Activity
Introduce the activity by saying, “Let’s see how well you 
remember the story.”. Divide the Ss into two teams. Show the 
Ss different pages from the Big Book and say a right or wrong 
statement. For example, “Pam, Paul and Grandpa are cleaning 
the attic. Is that right or wrong?”. The Ss should respond, 
“That’s wrong!” and then correct it by saying “Pam, Paul and 
Grandma are cleaning the attic.” The Ss can decide together as 
a group whether the phrase is true or false, but they must take 
turns to reply. Every time one of the teams answers correctly, 
they get a point.

> Advanced Groups
If you feel like your group is able to, let them come up with right 
or wrong statements about the story and ask their classmates 
about them.
6.– ACTIVITY 4: WHERE ARE YOU FROM? (7’) 
P.4.3
Italy
> How to Play
Ss must ask and answer questions about where they and their 
classmates are from according to the flash cards they pick up.
> Warm-Up
First, model the activity. Choose a Country flash card (P.4.3) 
and ask the Ss, “Can you guess where I’m from?”. Say for 
example, “Where I’m from, you can see Big Ben, people speak 
English, and it’s always rainy.”. The Ss must guess by asking, 
“Are you from England?” and then, you must respond by saying 
either “Yes, I am,” or “No, I am not.”
NOTE: if your Ss are familiar with the target language, you 
may skip this step.
> Main Activity
A Ss chooses a Country flash card (P.4.3) and keeps it a secret 
from the rest. The group then asks, “Where are you from?”. 
The S should give clues using the following structures:
•	 Where I’m from people speak…
•	 Where I’m from you can see…
•	 Where I’m from people eat…
•	 Where I’m from you can visit…
Ss must guess their classmate’s country by asking for 
example, “Are you from Australia?” to which the S should 
reply, “Yes, I am,” or “No, I am not.” Make sure that every S 
participates either by taking a country or by asking questions. 
As it can take a long time for all Ss to have a go at this activity

we recommend that you take a note of any Ss that didn’t get 
a go so they can go first the following day.
> Follow-Up
Ask Ss quick questions about the country they are from. 
Say, “What language do people speak where you are from?”, 
“What can you see there?”, “What do people eat?”, “What can 
you visit?”. Let the group come up with ideas and respond by 
saying: “Where I’m from…”
7.– ACTIVITY 6: TRAVEL TIPS (9’)
P.4.2
England
P.4.7
> How to Play
Ss should find matching pairs of countries (P.4.2) and the 
things that they can see or visit there (P.4.7). When they get a 
correct match, Ss must give advice on what to do there.
> Warm-Up
Take a country card (P.4.2) at random and say “I’m going to 
Japan. What should I visit?” to which Ss should reply, “If you 
go to Japan, you should visit Mount Fuji.” Try to quickly review 
at least five more countries.
NOTE: if your Ss are familiar with the target language, you 
may skip this step.
> Main Activity
Before class, prepare decks consisting of six cards: three 
countries, and three things you can do there (one per country). 
You will need as many decks as pairs of Ss in your group.
Put the Ss into pairs. Deal S1 the country cards and S2 the 
activity cards. S1 takes a country card and says for example, 
“I’m going to Italy. What should I visit?”. Then S2 looks for the 
corresponding card in their deck, shows it to their partner and 
says, “If you go to Italy, you should visit the Leaning Tower 
of Pisa.” Give each S at least two pairs to work on.

If time allows, redistribute the different decks and change 
their roles (from asking for advice to giving it, and vice versa).
> Follow-Up
Take two cards that don’t match and say for example, “If 
you go to Canada, you should visit the Eiffel Tower.”. Ss will 
see that it is not correct so encourage them to correct you by 
saying, “No, that’s wrong. If you go to Canada, you should 
see polar bears.”
NOTE: accept other options that the Ss might come up with, 
if they are correct and they use the proper structure.
8.– ACTIVITY 3: A TRIP AROUND THE WORLD (8’)
P.4.3
Italy
TARGET LANGUAGE
•	 Argentina: in this country people speak Spanish, you 
can have barbecues, and you can visit Patagonia.
•	 Australia: in this country people speak English, you 
can see kangaroos and visit the Great Barrier Reef.
•	 Brazil: in this country people speak Portuguese, you 
can visit Christ the Redeemer and go to the Amazon 
rainforest. 
•	 Canada: in this country people speak English and 
French; you can see polar bears and you can eat maple 
syrup.
•	 China: in this country people speak Chinese, you can 
eat noodles, and you can visit the Great Wall.
•	 Egypt: in this country people speak Arabic, you can 
visit the pyramids and the River Nile.
•	 England: in this country people speak English, you can 
visit Big Ben and the London Eye and it’s very rainy.
•	 France: in this country people speak French, you can 
eat cheese, and you can visit the Eiffel Tower or the 
Louvre Museum.
•	 Germany: in this country people speak German, you 
can eat sausages, and you can visit the Berlin Wall or 
go to the Black Forest.

•	 India: in this country people speak Hindi and English; 
you can eat curry, and you can visit the Taj Mahal.
•	 Italy: in this country people speak Italian, you can eat 
pizza, and you can visit the Colosseum or the Leaning 
Tower of Pisa.
•	 Japan: in this country people speak Japanese, you can 
visit Mount Fuji and many temples.
•	 Madagascar: in this country people speak Malagasy 
and French; you can see lemurs and baobab trees. 
•	 South Africa: in this country people speak English, you 
can see elephants and you can go on a safari.
•	 Spain: in this country people speak Spanish, you can 
visit the Sagrada Familia and the Alhambra.
•	 United States: in this country people speak English, you 
can visit the Grand Canyon and the Statue of Liberty.
> How to Play
Ss listen to descriptions of countries and throw paper airplanes 
at the correct flash cards. Before class, write the names of the 
countries on small pieces of scrap paper, fold them up and 
place them in a cloth bag.
> Main Activity
Stick the flash cards (P.4.3) up around the classroom (one 
flash card per S, or two if you have a small class).
A S chooses a piece of paper from the cloth bag and gives 
it to you without looking at it. Give clues to the S about that 
country saying for example, “In this country, people speak 
English, you can visit Big Ben and it’s very rainy.” The S must 
ask as many questions as needed to guess which country you’re 
describing by asking, for example, “Is it Egypt?”
When the S guesses correctly, all Ss can throw their airplanes 
at the correct country flash card. The group then walks over 
to where their airplanes are, collects them and stands next to 
that country while a new S gets a turn. Give them five for this 
transition. 
NOTE: if you find that a S is having difficulty guessing, allow 
the other Ss to help. However, once your Ss are used this activity 
they can play the teacher’s role and have their classmates 
guess which country they’re describing. 
> Follow-Up
Ask quick questions about the different countries. “In which 
country do people eat maple syrup? Where do they speak 
English and French? Where can you see polar bears?”. Ss 
must run to the country you’re describing and say, “In Canada!”

> Advanced Groups
You can let your Ss take turns being the teacher and giving 
clues to the rest of the group, who will have to guess which 
country they are describing.

10.– TIME TO GO HOME (TR#20) (2’) 
Sing the Time to Go Home song and have the Ss form a line 
before leaving the class. 
BONUS
PREPOSITIONS ACTION SONG (TR#9)
> Main Activity
Play the Prepositions Actions Song (TR#9) and dance to it. 
PREPOSITIONS ACTIONS SONG
(as you sing, simply perform the actions mentioned in the song. 
You can also create a hand choreography for the preposition 
verses.) 
In, on, under, next to, between, in front of, behind. 
In, on, under, next to, between, in front of, behind. 
Now stop.

March in line, in, in line. 
(musical interlude)
Hide under the table, under, under the table.  
In, on, under, next to, between, in front of, behind. 
In, on, under, next to, between, in front of, behind. 
Now stop.  
Walk next to a friend, next to, next to a friend. 
(musical interlude)
Stand between two chairs, between, between two chairs.  
In, on, under, next to, between, in front of, behind. 
In, on, under, next to, between, in front of, behind. 
Now stop.  
Jump behind the teacher, behind, behind the teacher. 
(musical interlude)
Run in front of the board, in front of, in front of the board.  
In, on, under, next to, between, in front of, behind. 
In, on, under, next to, between, in front of, behind. 
Now stop.  
Sit on a chair, on, on a chair. 
(musical interlude)
This is the end, the end, the end.
ACTIVITY 7: COUNTRIES MEMORY LOTTO
P.4.7
South Africa
China
Argentina
P.4.7
P.4.7
> How to Play
For this game, Ss must match the attractions on the Memory 
cards (P.4.7) with the countries on their Bingo boards (P.4.7).

> Main Activity
Give each S one Bingo board and place the Memory cards 
face down in the middle of the table. Introduce the activity by 
saying “Let’s talk about the places we travelled to and what 
we saw there!”
To play, a S turns over a memory card which shows something 
you can see or do in a certain country. 
If it is a match the S must say, “I went to South Africa to see 
elephants. It’s a pair. Can I have a counter, please?”
If it is not a match, they must say, “I didn’t go to South Africa 
to see kangaroos; I went to South Africa to see elephants. 
It’s not a pair.” 
Adapt the target language (eat, go, see, visit) as needed.
